Building a modern website usually means assembling a stack: a headless CMS, a framework, a host, a form service, an analytics vendor, an image CDN. Autoresearch

Turn Claude Code, OpenCode, OpenAI Codex, pi, or Muse into an improvement engine that keeps running without you.

The idea comes from Karpathy's autoresearch: give the agent a constraint, a mechanical metric, and autonomous iteration, and the gains compound.

You set the GOAL. The agent runs the LOOP. You wake up to results.

You don't need AGI. You need a goal, a metric, and a loop that never quits.

The core skill, bundled runtime, installation, and verification surface support Claude Code, OpenCode, OpenAI Codex, pi, and Muse. Hook guardrails are available for Claude Code (native hooks) and pi (extension events).

Fork-and-flush: metric loops escape plateaus the way Cai et al. (arXiv:2610.07447) do. At 33% and 66% of the budget, or after 5 iterations with no keep, the loop forks fresh-context branches from the best commit so far, runs each briefly, and keeps the winner. Half the branches pick their own ideas (randomness); the other half each get a distinct experiment from a stateless Advisor that reads the results log (Zhang et al., arXiv:2610.07625). Guided: R sets the split. When the orchestrator hits a plateau, it answers with FORK before it gives up. See guide/autoresearch.md.

Bumblebee is a read-only inventory collector for package, extension, and developer-tool metadata on macOS and Linux developer endpoints.

It answers one narrow supply-chain response question: when an advisory names a package, extension, or version, which developer machines show a match in their on-disk metadata right now?

SBOMs help answer what shipped, and EDR helps answer what ran or touched the network. Supply-chain response often needs a different view: messy local state across lockfiles, package-manager metadata, extension manifests, and supported developer-tool configs.

Bumblebee turns that scattered on-disk state into structured NDJSON component records. Given an exposure catalog, it flags exact matches for fast, read-only exposure checks when responders already know what they are looking for.

Claude-native first, Octopus for escalation. Use the Claude-native /init, /review, and /security-review when Claude is enough. Use Octopus when you want multiple model opinions, adversarial review, or stricter multi-LLM workflows.

Claude Octopus is an independent open-source project. It is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by Anthropic.

Research, build, review, and ship with twelve external providers checking the host's work. The Claude-native path handles ordinary tasks. Octopus stays dormant until you explicitly run /octo:*, then takes over the escalated path. A 75% consensus gate catches disagreements before they reach production.

It remembers across sessions. Integrations with claude-mem, agentmemory, and deja-vu provide persistent memory, so past decisions, research, and context survive session boundaries.

Spec in, software out. Dark Factory mode takes a spec and runs the full pipeline on its own: research, define, develop, deliver. You review the output instead of every step.

Pick the workflow the task needs. Use a focused method for architecture, debugging, or TDD. Use /octo:embrace for Discover, Define, Develop, Deliver, with quality gates between phases.

ACI: Open-Source Infra to Power Unified MCP Servers and VibeOps

It gives agents intent-aware access to tools with multi-tenant auth, granular permissions, and tool discovery, exposed either as direct function calls or through a Unified Model-Context-Protocol (MCP) server.

As an example: rather than writing separate OAuth flows and API clients for Google Calendar, Slack, and other services, you can use ACI.dev to handle authentication and give AI agents unified, secure function calls. You can reach these capabilities through our Unified MCP server or through our lightweight Python SDK, which works with any LLM framework.

Add a single unified MCP server to your favourite agentic IDE to speed up vibe coding and automate devOps. Configure the MCP with Vercel, Supabase, Cloudflare, and other platforms. SkillsBench is a benchmark that tests whether AI agents can use Skills to complete professional tasks across different domains. It measures how much a model improves at solving complex real-world tasks when it has specialized Skills available.

To test performance in production-like environments where many Skills are installed at once, we adapted SkillsBench into a large-scale multi-Skill setting. In the original setup, each task comes with only the Skill for that task. In our modified setting, every task is evaluated in a global environment containing all 195 specialized Skills, with all other experimental conditions unchanged. The point is to see whether an agent can find, select, and combine the right Skills from a large installed pool, and build them into an effective workflow for completing complex tasks.

We benchmarked vibeskills v4.1.0 on SkillsBench, using DeepSeekV4Flash-VE and OpenHands as the baseline evaluation setup. Compared with the baseline without vibeskills, vibeskills raised the mean verifier reward by 21.12 percentage points, cut token consumption by 29.6%, and reduced tool calls by 33.1%.

Releases

sem is a semantic version control tool that runs on top of Git. It parses your code with tree-sitter, extracts every function, class, and method as an entity, and diffs at the entity level instead of lines. So you see "function blahh was modified" instead of "lines x-y changed."

It works in any Git repo with no setup.
